data.title: US futures climb and Asian shares mostly decline as some tech stocks fall
data.description:
Asian shares were mostly lower Monday (Nov 23) after a brutal sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent on Friday.

But US stock futures climbed early Monday. The future for the S&P 500 was up 2.1 per cent early Monday, while the future for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.5 per cent.

Some big AI stocks helped pull Asian shares down. South Korea's benchmark Kospi index fell 3.3 per cent to 4,708.54 even as it narrowed some of its losses from earlier in the day. Shares in Samsung Electronics lost 3.1 per cent, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix fell 2.5 per cent.

Markets in Tokyo were closed for a holiday.

Taiwan's Taiex added 2.2 per cent. Its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., was up 1.5 per cent.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1 per cent lower to 22,389.18, while the Shanghai Composite index was 0.2 per cent higher at 3,538.95.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.3 per cent lower to 8,570.60.

India's Sensex dropped 1.1 per cent.

After Friday's decline, Wall Street's benchmark S&P 500 is now in what professional investors call a "correction", having fallen more than 10 per cent from its Oct 6 all-time high. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite slumped 5.3 per cent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. The Dow fell 1.9 per cent.

US-traded shares of AI-related stocks including Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5 per cent.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the past 10, closing 14 per cent lower.

The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI buildout and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. 

Since the scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30 per cent.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among US consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to October, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. 

Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the US war with Iran.

In commodities trading, oil prices fell early Monday, as a recovery in supply continued to help offset concerns even as the US and Iran have yet to reach a permanent deal over the war. 

Analysts are expecting oil and fuel prices to fall further as global supply stabilises, which could help ease some inflationary pressures.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, lost 0.4 per cent to $92.21 per barrel, but that's still well above the roughly US$72 ($93) a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Benchmark US crude slipped 0.3 per cent to US$83.14 per barrel.

The US dollar rose to 158.93 Japanese yen from 158.62 yen. The euro climbed to US$1.1003 from US$1.10973.

data.title: Singapore's core inflation drops to 1.5% in October, but is expected to rise in Q1 2027
data.description:
Singapore's core inflation dropped to 1.5 per cent year-on-year in October, down from the 2 per cent recorded in September, data from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) showed.

This was because of lower inflation for services and electricity and gas, METI and MAS said in a joint media release on Nov 23 (Monday).

On a month-on-month basis, core prices — which exclude accommodation and private transport due to their volatility and tendency to be influenced by supply-side administrative policies — were unchanged from September.

Overall inflation, listed as "Consumer Price Index-All Items" eased by 0.3 percentage points, to 1.9 per cent year-on-year in October, due to a fall in private transport inflation alongside lower core inflation.

MTI and MAS said overall inflation, on a month-on-month basis, dropped by 0.3 per cent in October.

This excludes non-consumption expenditure such as purchases of houses, shares and other financial assets and income taxes.

Breakdown by sector

The data showed that electricity and gas inflation fell the most — from 8.7 per cent in September to 1 per cent in October. 

MAS and METI said this was largely due to the lower regulated electricity tariff in the month, pointing to the lower global energy prices over the period of July to mid-September. 

Services, private transport and food inflation moderated by 0.6, 0.4, and 0.1 percentage points, to 1.1, 6.7, and 2.3 per cent respectively. 

These were due to smaller increases in airfares as well as the costs of health insurance and healthcare services, a more gradual increase in car prices, and prices of non-cooked food rising at a slower pace.

Meanwhile, accommodation inflation remained unchanged at 0.9 per cent.

But inflation for retail and other goods rose from 1.2 per cent in September to 1.6 per cent in October as furniture prices rose and household appliance prices fell at a slower pace.

Outlook

The ministry and authority noted that energy commodity prices have eased recently, but cautioned that they remain volatile and elevated compared to a year ago.

Global and regional food prices are also expected to pick up as costlier inputs and adverse weather patterns affect food production.

Nonetheless, METI and MAS expect imported inflation to ease next year as the effects of temporary supply disruptions fade.

Meanwhile, domestic price pressures are expected to stay subdued, with unit labour costs in the services sector expected to remain contained amid continued productivity gains.

"Enhanced government subsidies, such as for healthcare and education, will also dampen services inflation," METI and MAS said.

Core inflation expected to pick up

Core inflation is expected to average between 1.5 and 2 per cent in 2026, and between 1.5 and 2.5 per cent next year.

METI and MAS said they expect core inflation to pick up in the first quarter of 2027, before easing "more discernibly" from the middle of next year.

"The risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside," METI and MAS stated, explaining that a sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore's import costs by more than projected. 

Domestic inflation could also stay elevated if spillovers from the artificial intelligence-related boom broaden and unit labour costs rise more rapidly.

But higher-than-expected global interest rates or a pullback in AI-related investment could also exert a drag on growth, and thus, inflation.

Energy prices could also decline faster if production and shipments from the Middle East recover more quickly than projected, they said.

data.title: South Korea vows to stabilise stock market after KOSPI drops 5%
data.description:
SEJONG — South Korea reiterated plans on Monday (Nov 23) to stabilise its stock market if needed, as the KOSPI plummeted five per cent and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il projected solid economic growth next year.

The benchmark index extended declines as concerns over the AI trade and a broader technology selloff overwhelmed the government's assurances that stabilisation funds would be deployed immediately if conditions worsened.

"Given the high impact of external uncertainties, volatility in our stock market has expanded significantly, which is why we addressed the issue. The message we delivered yesterday is that we will decide whether to activate measures depending on market conditions," Lee said at a press conference in Sejong.

"Accordingly, we are preparing so that necessary steps tailored to the situation will be implemented at an appropriate time."

On Sunday, the authorities said they would deploy market stabilisation funds immediately if conditions deteriorated, after the South Korean benchmark index tumbled to a 10-month low last week.

Lee said Asia's fourth-largest economy was maintaining strong momentum and could achieve growth in the upper-three per cent range if present trends continued.

Despite the upbeat baseline outlook, Lee warned that external risks remained severe, citing regulatory uncertainty surrounding the artificial intelligence industry, geopolitical instability and rising global interest rates. 

He cautioned that volatility in the semiconductor sector could spill over and amplify broader macroeconomic swings.

Asked whether South Korea could revise rules related to short-selling, Lee said the government's plan was to place greater emphasis on cracking down on illegal short-selling and strengthening surveillance against unfair trading rather than pursuing additional deregulation.

South Korea imposed a blanket short-selling ban in late 2023 to curb market volatility and illegal trading, lifting the 17-month prohibition in March 2025 after launching a centralised detection system.

Source: Reuters

data.title: A Clementi 4-room HDB flat just sold for a record $1.38m despite being on a lower floor
data.description:
A four-room flat at Clementi Crest has just been sold for $1.38 million, the highest price for a four-room resale flat in Clementi. At $1,379 psf, it is also the highest psf for a four-room flat in the town.

The 1,001 sq ft Model A unit at Block 445B Clementi Avenue 3, between the 28th and 30th floors, changed hands this week. It has about 94 years left on its lease.

The previous town record was also set at Clementi Crest, at the neighbouring Block 445A. That 1,001 sq ft flat, between the 37th and 39th floors, sold for $1.356 million ($1,354 psf) in August 2026.

What's interesting is that the new record is the same size as the flat it beat and sits nine floors lower, yet it sold for about $24,000 more.

A mid-floor flat that outpriced the higher floor units

The record price isn't obvious from the flat's attributes alone. The 28th to 30th floors are not near the top of the development. All five of the next-highest four-room sales in Clementi were on the 31st floor or higher, and the flat which claimed the previous record sat between the 37th and 39th floors.

Size doesn't explain it either. The record flat, the previous record and the other four top resales in Clementi are all 1,001 sq ft. So the $24,000 gap is like-for-like, and the psf price increases from $1,354 to $1,379.

The lease also doesn't distinguish them. The new record has 93 years and eight months left, against 93 years and 11 months for the previous record. Both round to about 94 years.

Clementi Crest was completed in 2020, which makes it about six years old. Block 445B has 193 flats made up of 115 four-room and 78 five-room units. At around 60per cent of the block, four-room flats aren't an unusually rare flat type there.

Within Block 445B, the next-highest sale was a 1,001 sq ft unit on the 31st to 33rd floors, which went for about $1.3 million in January 2026. Another unit on the same 28th to 30th floors also changed hands for $1.3 million in May 2026. The new record is about $80,000 above both, and it came about six months after the May sale.

Notably, the five highest sales in the block before this record deal all range between $1.28 million and $1.30 million.

All five were sold along Clementi Avenue 4 in November 2026, and fetched prices that range from $1.01 million to $1.095 million. Four of them are smaller flats of 861 to 883 sq ft.

The one 1,001 sq ft flat in the table, at Block 312C on the 10th to 12th floors, sold for $1.085 million. The new record is about $295,000 above that, so it is an exceptional sale, even against other recent four-room sales in Clementi.

Over the past 12 months, the median resale price for four-room flats in Clementi was $800,000, based on 226 transactions. Prices ranged from $455,000 to the new record of $1.38 million. That puts the record transaction about $580,000 above the median resale price for this type of flat in Clementi.

Most four-room flats in the town change hands well below $1 million. A flat completed in 2020 with about 94 years left on its lease is likely to sit at the longer-lease end of what is sold in Clementi, which may help explain the price gap.

However, this isn't the most expensive four-room flat in Singapore. That is the $1.588 million sale at Block 1A Cantonment Road at The Pinnacles @ Duxton, which sold in October 2026. Nevertheless, the record sale at Clementi Crest is an exceptional transaction in the town, and a milestone for the town's HDB resale market.

data.title: Anthropic's record IPO raises hopes for a charitable windfall that has nonprofits preparing to scale
data.description:
NEW YORK — It was philanthropy, the story goes, that first bonded two of the founders behind artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

Jared Kaplan, the San Francisco company's chief science officer, and CEO Dario Amodei were doctoral students carpooling to an event organised by an academic fellowship. As Kaplan recalls, he and Amodei spent the ride discussing "this idea of thoroughly investigating what kinds of charitable causes could do the most good".

"We had so much largesse to, sort of, disperse," Kaplan joked at a Hertz Foundation discussion in April 2025.

Those once-hypothetical philanthropic ambitions gained new steam as Anthropic debuted on the stock market to a record US$1.5 trillion (S$1.9 trillion) valuation. 

The Claude AI tool maker already plans to dedicate five per cent of its shares for a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Its seven co-founders say they'll give away 80 per cent of their equity — a US$112 billion commitment based on its IPO price.

Now suddenly affluent employees, many of whom will become millionaires as they sell their vested stock, may wield enough capital to make transformative donations themselves - riches that are commanding the attention of nonprofits looking to direct some sliver toward causes from global health to animal welfare.

Silicon Valley has great expectations. The napkin math suggests leading US AI firms' valuations could add at least US$37 billion annually in intended philanthropy, according to a widely circulated May blog post by Nan Ransohoff, head of public goods at the payments company Stripe.

"This is a once-in-a-lifetime kind of opportunity for people to really make an impact on extreme poverty," said Peter Singer, the moral philosopher whose writings influence many tech donors.

Nonprofits aren't counting on an immediate charitable windfall, though. Many Anthropic employees cannot sell or gift the bulk of their shares until next spring. 

Questions persist about the charitable priorities of these potential philanthropists whose worldviews have been shaped by the increasingly powerful AI models advancing at breakneck speed. 

The sector's volatility — between high borrowing costs, recent turmoil at the chipmaker Nvidia and warnings about risks to humanity — leaves skeptics doubtful about the amounts actually available to redistribute.

"The challenge is that deploying philanthropic capital is hard," said Renaissance Philanthropy president Kumar Garg, whose nonprofit matches funders with scientific initiatives. "That's not an automatic step."

AI philanthropists are expected to make large donations quickly

Will the artificial intelligence wave of wealth creation differ from previous ones that created new philanthropy?

There's reason to believe so, according to Benjamin Soskis, a historian of philanthropy and senior research associate at the Urban Institute's Center on Nonprofits and Philanthropy, even if he finds the number of tech executives who have "actually managed to empty the safe" is low.

The modern philanthropic foundation stemmed from the post-Civil War wave of industrial capitalism. Titans such as oil magnate John D. Rockefeller Sr. and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie established bureaucratic institutions intended to address the root causes of social problems. 

Those were followed by the turn-of-the-century technology wealth that brought a more data-centric, risk-taking approach. The Gates Foundation launched to address pressing crises in global health and poverty.

AI wealth, according to Soskis, carries a sense of "extreme peril" and "really transformative promise" that should spur even more urgent action from this emerging class of donors.

At least one of Anthropic's co-founders will donate in the coming weeks to the Trump Accounts children's savings programme, according to comments made Friday by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on CNBC.

Anthropic's explosive growth is also fueling some anticipation that its 5,300 employees will want to rapidly scale their charitable impact, too. A generous internal giving programme adds another incentive. 

Employee equity gifts are matched by the company with shares of Class N common stock. Anthropic also partners with donor-advised fund vendors such as Daffy, which offer a tax-efficient tool for grantmaking without the hassle of a more sophisticated charitable foundation.

Daffy CEO Adam Nash expects this younger generation to give more quickly.

"The people working in AI see the impact AI is having already," Nash said. "And they are giving now, right?"

Tech-adjacent nonprofits prepare for influx

One organisation in particular appears poised to move those rising donation volumes.

Coefficient Giving was formed by San Francisco-based billionaire Cari Tuna and her husband, Dustin Moskovitz, a Facebook co-founder and early Anthropic investor. A spokesperson told The New York Times the couple transferred their Anthropic stake into an undisclosed nonprofit last year to avoid personally profiting.

The philanthropic funder — which has directed more than US$8 billion since 2014 in support of global health, animal rights, AI safety and the effective altruism community — has been scaling its pledges. In July, Coefficient Giving increased its commitment to the grantmaker GiveWell to US$1 billion.

The move reflected expectations of "considerably more future funding for this kind of work," according to the announcement.

"We might grow a lot, in part because we want to spend faster in response to these trends," Coefficient Giving CEO Alexander Berger said during a late July public discussion. 

"But there is a great deal of room for other organisations and approaches, and I do not expect us to play an overwhelmingly dominant role."

GiveDirectly has spent months identifying the biggest barriers to rapidly growing its antipoverty work, according to Nick Allardice, its president and CEO. The tech-focused nonprofit sends cash straight to poor households with no strings attached.

Recipients must have mobile phones to receive the digital transfers. GiveDirectly offers phones for about US$15, usually subtracted from recipients' first payment. So the nonprofit secured investments this year to build out a supply chain to support many more mobile phones going forward.

The group is betting that its preparations for a charitable boom will be worthwhile.

"I have this level of cautious optimism," Allardice said. "But I can't foresee the future, and I don't know exactly what's going to happen."

Wild Animal Initiative executive director Cameron Meyer Shorb shares those tempered expectations.

His nonprofit funds wild animal welfare research. It's the sort of work some observers predict will see the biggest upswings in support: nonprofits connected to effective altruism, a data-driven movement that prioritises donations to causes with the greatest impact on the most living beings.

The movement's reputation took a hit when Sam Bankman-Fried, one of its leading proponents and financial backers, got a 25-year prison sentence for cryptocurrency fraud. But the ideas are rebounding in the same tech circles that could see big payouts as more AI companies go public.

Effective altruists have learned not to rely too heavily on any one funder, according to Shorb. He expects "quite a bit" of fresh support for animal advocacy and sees an outsize role for midsize donors.

He said he has connected with a couple of Anthropic employees. Perhaps more important, he said, are relationships with the philanthropic advisers who help plan donors' giving.

"As you can imagine, it's a pretty tricky place for a soon-to-be billionaire to be to have all this potential power coming soon," Shorb said. "As soon as anyone finds out about that, anyone who can possibly get their email or phone number will just be knocking down their door. So we've tried to be gentle and slow and respectful in our approach."

data.title: Oil prices fall amid equity selloff though Iran war attacks limit losses
data.description:
PERTH — Oil prices fell on Monday (Nov 23) as the selloff in the wider financial markets amid concerns about the ability of the AI sector to boost economic growth spilled over into commodities, though the continuing attacks on Gulf shipping limited the losses.

Crude dropped, adding to its three-week losing streak, amid the overall negative sentiment in global financial markets as Asian equities opened lower on Monday, with the tech-heavy South Korean market down four per cent and China, Hong Kong and Australia all falling. US equity markets have also slumped with the Nasdaq plunging 10 per cent last week.

Brent crude futures fell 28 cents, or 0.30 per cent, to US$92.29 (S$120) a barrel by 2.16am GMT (10.16am SGT). US West Texas Intermediate futures fell 15 cents, or 0.18 per cent, to us$83.26 a barrel.

Brent declined four per cent last week and WTI five per cent.

Still, the fighting from the unresolved US-Israeli war against Iran continues to limit any losses. On Sunday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery and over the weekend multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of Hormuz were reported.

"It's momentum carrying (oil) down," said Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at Sydney-based XAnalysts. But he cautioned that the shipping attacks are having an effect as "ballast (empty) vessels counts are building in crude while laden vessels are not. This risk to flows will start to price soon".

In Turkey, talks on Sunday at the global climate summit COP31 collapsed for the first time since 2009 after nations could not come to an agreement over including a statement on the phase-out of fossil fuels in a final text.

Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing countries have said fossil fuels will play a role in the economy for the foreseeable future and they lobbied to keep any mention of fossil fuels out of the text, observers at the summit said.

OPEC had earlier defended fossil fuel use at the summit.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

data.title: CPF Board, Singtel complete transfer of special discounted shares to CDP accounts
data.description:
Holders of Singtel's Special Discounted Shares (SDS) can now hold and manage their shares directly, following the completion of transfer from CPF Board to the Central Depository (CDP) on Nov 21.

In an joint news release on Monday (Nov 23), Singtel Group and CPF Board said that about 406,000 of the 615,000 SDS holders have transferred 477 million SDS to their CDP accounts.

Meanwhile, about 209,000, or 34 per cent, sold their shares.

"Leading up to the transfer, CPF Board and Singtel worked closely to reach out to SDS holders through individual notifications as well as various publicity and outreach efforts, including in-person and online touchpoints," they added.

CPF Board and Singtel reiterated that no action is needed for those who wish to continue holding their Singtel SDS, noting that designated CDP accounts have been created for about one-third of the 406,000, who were without an account.

Those holding individual CDP accounts will now have their Singtel SDS consolidated with other securities in their CDP accounts and any other Singtel ordinary shares they may be holding.

If they wish to sell their Singtel SDS, they can do so via an SGX-registered brokerage that they have a trading account with. 

As for SDS holders with designated CDP accounts created in their name, they can sell their shares through Philip Securities website, in person at SingPost, or select SGX retail brokers.

Notification and scam advisory

All SDS holders will receive a hardcopy notification letter from CPF Board, CDP and Singtel by mid-December, informing them of the transfer completion.

CPF Board also advised its members to remain vigilant against scams, noting that some scammers may fabricate stories about members' Singtel SDS to deceive them.

The board advised those who received messages, email, or QR code which allegedly directs them to the SDS website to first verify the URL's authenticity. The official website is https://sds.singtel.com. 

Singtel's group chief financial officer Arthur Lang said the transfer of SDs shares to CDP accounts was ultimately about giving holders a choice and enabling them to exercise their rights as shareholders directly.

"As we move forward, our focus remains on executing our strategy, investing for sustainable growth and creating long-term value for all our shareholders," he added.

data.title: Annual Value thresholds for social support schemes to be raised from March 2027
data.description:
The Government will raise the Annual Value (AV) thresholds used to determine eligibility for social support schemes from March 1, 2027, announced the Ministry of Finance (MOF) on Monday (Nov 23).

The move intends to ensure that Singaporeans living in HDB flats and lower-value private properties will continue to qualify for a range of support schemes as the AV of many residential properties increased since 2025, when the AVs were last adjusted, said MOF.

By adjusting the thresholds, the Government aims to ensure that Singaporeans with greater needs do not lose access to support schemes solely because of higher property valuations.

The AV of a home, alongside other criteria such as income, is one of several indicators used to assess eligibility and determine the level of benefits an individual or household may receive under schemes including the GST Voucher scheme, MediShield Life premium subsidies and the Workfare Income Supplement scheme.

Those living in properties with lower AVs generally receive higher levels of support.

Currently, households fall into two AV tiers: Homes with an AV of up to $21,000, and homes with an AV of more than $21,000 but not exceeding $31,000. 

From March 1, 2027, the thresholds will be revised upwards. 

The first AV tier will increase to up to $24,000, while the second AV tier will rise to more than $24,000 and up to $32,000.

Eligibility for social support schemes in a given year is based on the preceding year's AV. 

This means that eligibility for 2027 benefits will be assessed using a household's or individual's 2026 AV.

The Government said it will continue reviewing its social support schemes and eligibility criteria to ensure support remains targeted at Singaporeans with greater needs.

Singaporeans seeking more information can approach the respective government agencies administering the various schemes.

data.title: One-off property tax rebate for all owner-occupied residential properties in 2027
data.description:
Homeowners in Singapore will receive a one-off property tax rebate in 2027, with HDB flat owners getting a 15 per cent reduction and private residential property owners receiving a 10 per cent rebate capped at $100.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) and The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (Iras) announced the rebates on Monday (Nov 23), saying the move aims to cushion property tax payments amid cost-of-living concerns.

The rebates will be automatically offset against the property tax payable in homeowners' 2027 tax bills.

After the rebates, owner-occupiers living in three-room and larger HDB flats can expect to pay an average of about $2 to $4 more in property tax per month.

Most owner-occupiers of private residential properties will see an average increase of about $6 per month.

Those living in one-room and two-room HDB flats will continue to pay no property tax.

HDB flat values updated to reflect market rents

As part of its annual review, the Government has updated the Annual Values (AVs) of HDB flats to better reflect prevailing market rents in their respective towns.

Property tax bills are due by Jan 31, 2027.

All property owners will receive their 2027 property tax bills by December 2026.

Iras will notify property owners via SMS and/or email when their bills are available for viewing on the myTax Portal.

As the tax bills will be issued in batches, some homeowners may receive theirs earlier than others.

The payment deadline is Jan 31, 2027.

Property owners are encouraged to pay through GIRO, either in interest-free monthly instalments of up to 12 months or through a one-time deduction.

Eligible retiree owner-occupiers aged 65 and above, with an assessable income of $39,000 or below, may apply for an extended GIRO instalment plan of up to 24 months to make their payments.
